# Canary — islam.museum release notes

The museum's public release notes: every change that lands on `main`, recorded in
reader's language in the same commit that makes the change. Newest release first.
The site build reads the version and date from the top block below and shows them
in the footer of every page and on the changelog page (`/{lang}/changelog/`).

Rules for every agent and contributor (`docs/engineering/15-release-notes-and-versioning.md`):
append your entry under the current version block, grouped by kind — Added, Changed,
Fixed, Removed, Performance, Tests, Data, Breaking, Rolled back. Write what changed
and why it matters, never a bare commit message. If your change bumps the version,
open a new block on top with the new version and today's date.

---

## v1.30.1 — 2026-11-14
### Added
- **Enrichment register: one place to find every record and prose file that still needs work.** `npm run enrichment-queue` derives the gaps live from the graph (missing Wikidata, VIAF, OpenITI, Biblissima, GeoNames, Pleiades and iDAI ids; missing, partial and draft-only Arabic, English and Urdu prose; records with no or one weak source; persons without birth or death, places without coordinates, events without dates, works without author or date; wanted stubs) and writes ranked shards under `docs/library/enrichment/queue/`, so an idle agent can take the next most-referenced item. `claims.yaml` records who has taken what, and `npm run check:enrichment-register` (part of `npm run validate`) fails on two claims on the same items. Rule added to `AGENTS.md`.
- **Yaqut's Mu'jam al-Buldan on seven more place pages (packet 70).** Mardin, al-Ladhiqiyya, Fadak, al-Shaykhan, Cordoba, Arqa and Sarakusta gain a cited Yaqut section in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft); Sarakusta gets its first prose pages. Sur, Rumah and Hungary were skipped because Yaqut's headword is a different place or absent.
- **Yaqut's Mu'jam al-Buldan now speaks on nine more place pages (packet 69).** Dhamar, al-Qulzum, Arrajan, al-Nujayr, Baza, Zam, Baeza, Tyre and Caesarea each gain a cited section in Arabic, English and Urdu summarising what Yaqut says of them (draft), and the data files list the Sader edition as a source. Al-Jafar was skipped because its identity is unclear.
- **Harvest register: one central file records every book, audio series, website and dataset processed so far.** `docs/library/harvest-register.yaml` (with `docs/library/README.md` and a fast `npm run check:harvest-register` check, wired into `npm run validate`) lets any agent see what is downloaded, OCRed, mined and ingested before redoing work, and sets a deletion gate: a finished book's PDF may leave the microSD only after its OCR text is zipped and verified. AGENTS.md and the agent guides point to it. Nothing was deleted.
- **Yaqut's Mu'jam al-Buldan now speaks on seven more place pages (packet 68).** Cordoba, Adhruh, Raydah, Harasta, Samasta, Haditha (of the Euphrates) and Sabalan each gain an Arabic, English and Urdu section summarising Yaqut's entry, cited to the Dar Sader volume and page. Cordoba, Harasta and Haditha get their first prose page. Three cards (Oman, al-Sayla, al-Miyanij) were skipped because Yaqut's headword is a different or unclear place; they are logged for outside research.

### Fixed
- **Eight published person cards now say which prose is AI text awaiting a human read.** Alqama ibn Abada, Talha ibn Tahir, Taha al-Jibrini, Talha ibn Musarrif, Tannus al-Shidyaq, Tawwaf ibn Ghallaq, Zafir al-Sukkari and Zahir al-Umar keep their published status, and each gets an `ai_unread` note for the al-A'lam sections added on 14 November 2026. Leftover merge-conflict markers in the web-sources progress file were removed with both sides kept.
- **Eight person cards corrected against al-Zirikli's al-A'lam and Wikidata (Lane B corrections, packet corr-p2).** Muhammad ibn Mustafa al-Bakri now carries his own dates (1143 to 1196 AH, 1731 to 1782; Jerusalem and Gaza) instead of his father's, Arabzade and Jafar ibn Ulba al-Harithi gain sourced dates (919 to 969 AH; d. 145 AH), Abd al-Haqq al-Dihlawi records al-A'lam's one-year difference, Abd Allah ibn Yusuf is named al-Tinnisi with his death in 218 AH from Shadharat al-Dhahab, the Omani poet Ahmad ibn al-Nadr takes 655 to 690 AH from Arabic Wikipedia and Wikidata (kept apart from al-Naysaburi), the physician Ibrahim ibn Abdallah loses an impossible tenth-century date (now sixteenth century, century precision), and the Ibn al-Daya card records an unresolved conflict between sources. Why it matters: a wrong date or a merged identity misleads every reader of the card.

- **The museum's block on terrorist-organisation content now covers the last seven designated names in full.** On the founder's ruling, Ansarallah (the Houthis), Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Ansar Dine, Hizb ut-Tahrir, Ansar al-Islam and the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood are now caught by the build's extremism check, under a complete ban: no propaganda material about them, in support of them or from them anywhere in the museum, in existing records or in future ones. Every existing record was audited mention by mention before the check was widened, and none contains any such material; the neutral historical mentions that remain (a corps commander's biography, a Nobel laureate's exile, a film that condemns the group it depicts) are recorded as the founder's exceptions, and two unrelated bodies that share a name — a Malian Sufi movement and a Nigerian society — are protected as non-matches. The content-safety rule now also lists where each of the seven classifications comes from, with the official designation lists' addresses. One name, Al-Andalus Media, is designated and banned in full, but its automatic check awaits the founder's ruling on a single ambiguous company name in one existing record.
- **The deeds calculator is now one screen you can use without reading anything.** The Hasanat and Sayyi'at Ledger (`/hisab/`) opens on large cards, one per act a text names a figure for, each with a single "Add" button; what you add is listed like a basket and the sums follow at once in a bar at the foot of the screen, with one clear colour per kind (good deeds, bad deeds, erasure, ranks). The counter, the full table with its texts, the ladder, the list of every counting text and the page's caveat and method are all still there, folded under "More on this page". The sums are still never subtracted from one another, and a result a text does not number is still shown in its words (plan 50 section 5).

- **Date and identity corrections on thirteen cards, each read in a primary source first (Lane B corrections, packet corr-p3, 14 November 2026).** Sadreddinzade al-Shirwani died on 3 Dhu al-Hijja 1036 AH, 15 August 1627 (TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi vol. 39), so the 1626 in his summary and prose is replaced. Sultan ibn Saif I was chosen imam in 1059 AH (1649), straight after Imam Nasir ibn Murshid's death on 22 April 1649 (Badger's translation of the Omani chronicle, pp. 74 and 77-78), not 1050 AH as al-A'lam prints it. The 242 AH death of Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Kharrash is kept: the 283 AH date proposed from outside belongs to a different man, Abd al-Rahman ibn Yusuf ibn Kharrash.

- **Twenty-five Canon of Medicine concepts on water, wine, sleep, weak organs and fatigue (Lane A, scan pages 236 to 244).** Book I, Fann 3, Ta'lim 2, chapters 8 to 13 of Ibn Sina's common regimen: water for balanced temperaments, drinking on an empty stomach and false thirst, the temperature of water, wine by temperament, with food, on the humours, old and new, mixed, by age and climate, foods and drinks that slow intoxication, sobering, wine for painful treatment, moderate sleep, Galen's lettuce, sleep timing, day and night sleep, sleeping positions, what is deferred to the particular books, strengthening weak organs, the kinds and causes of fatigue and stretching and yawning. Each concept has full Arabic, English and Urdu prose (draft, provenance-stamped) citing the printed volume and page. Garbled passages of the scan are left out and noted in the text.
- **Eighteen Canon of Medicine concepts on treating fatigue and the states after exercise (Lane A, scan pages 244 to 250).** Book I, Fann 3, Ta'lim 2, chapters 14 to 17 of Ibn Sina's common regimen, which closes the second teaching: the treatment of ulcerous, tension, inflammatory and desiccatory exercise fatigue, ripening raw matter with rubbing and oils, fatigue from movement and the bath test, raw humours in the intestinal vessels, expansion and condensation after exercise with their signs and remedies, weakness after excess, excess moisture from bathing and ease, spontaneous fatigue (where it lies, the regimen with the humour inside the vessels, raw humours in the principal organs, both together, tension and inflammatory kinds with venesection and three days of food), why refeeding after evacuation must be gradual, and bodies of imperfect temperament, mistaken and congenital. Each concept has full Arabic, English and Urdu prose (draft, provenance-stamped) citing the printed volume and page. Garbled passages are left out and noted in the text. Book I continues at Ta'lim 3, the regimen of the old (scan page 251).
- **Sixteen Canon of Medicine concepts on the regimen of the old and of unbalanced temperaments (Lane A, scan pages 251 to 257).** Book I, Fann 3, Ta'lim 3 and Ta'lim 4 of Ibn Sina's common regimen: the general regimen of the old, their feeding, milk, vegetables, fruits and gentle laxatives, keeping the bowels soft by enema and mild purging, wine, opening obstructions, rubbing and exercise; then the regimen of the excessively hot temperament (kinds, aims, diet, bath, evacuation and opening remedies), the hot and moist, the excessively cold, bodies quick to receive disease, fattening the emaciated and slimming the fat. Each concept has full Arabic, English and Urdu prose (draft, provenance-stamped) citing the printed volume and page. Garbled words of the scan are left out and noted in the text. Book I continues at scan page 258 (Fann 3, Ta'lim 5, the regimen of the seasons).
- **Twenty-four Canon of Medicine concepts on the regimen of the seasons, of corrupted air and of the traveller (Lane A, scan pages 258 to 266).** Book I, Fann 3, Ta'lim 5, which closes Fann 3: the regimen of spring, summer, autumn and winter, illness in winter and Hippocrates on purging, the regimen in corrupted air and epidemic with the fumigants and vinegar, then the eight chapters on the traveller (warning signs before disease, change of habit, signs pointing to particular organs, the general regimen of the traveller, training for hunger and thirst, travel in heat and the samum wind, drinking by sips, travel in cold, protecting and treating frostbitten limbs, the complexion, clarifying and correcting bad waters, and the sea traveller). Each is a trilingual draft (ar, en, ur) cited to the printed page, so readers can follow Ibn Sina's advice for health on the move season by season. Garbled OCR phrases are left out and listed in `docs/delegation/canon-ibn-sina-progress.md`.
- **Twenty-five Canon of Medicine concepts on the general principles of treatment, bad temperament and evacuation (Lane A, scan pages 267 to 276).** Book I, Fann 4 opens: the three means of treatment, withholding and reducing food, feeding in acute and chronic diseases, the speed and consistency of food, the three rules of drug treatment, reckoning a dose from the organ's temperament, build, position and strength, drawing matter away, sensitive and principal organs, the stage of the disease, changing drugs, pain and the mind, then the second chapter on treating bad temperament (cooling and heating compared, excess heat and obstructions, mixing a drug with its opposite) and the third on how and when to evacuate. Each is a trilingual draft (ar, en, ur) cited to the printed page, so readers can follow how Ibn Sina reasons from the patient and the organ to the remedy. Garbled OCR phrases are left out and listed in `docs/delegation/canon-ibn-sina-progress.md`.
- **Yaqut sections for eight places (packet 56).** Manbij, al-Jiza, Surraq, Dumat al-Jandal, Antaliya, Nishapur and Baykand gain a cited section on what Yaqut says of them in the Mu'jam al-Buldan (Dar Sader), and Santiago de Compostela gets its first page, in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft). Basta (Baza) and Urgench were skipped: Yaqut's entries describe a desert tract and the old Khwarazm capital, not our records.
- **Ten place cards gain a section from Yaqut's Mu'jam al-Buldan in Arabic, English and Urdu (packet 55).** al-Dabba, Amul (the Oxus town), al-Fayyum, Busra (Hawran), Qasr Masmuda, Shiltish, Amman (al-Balqa), al-Jar, Jurzan and al-Ahkaf each summarise, with page citations, what Yaqut says of the place: spelling, location, etymology, history and attributed reports. Why it matters: readers see the classical geographer's own account beside the other sources.
- **Three people read from the dictionaries, five cards corrected (Lane B2, packet id, identity re-check).** Short cited biographies in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft): Ibn al-Sikkit (al-A'lam 8:195, 186-244 AH, 802-858 CE; the earlier skip had matched the wrong entry), Ruh ibn Hatim al-Muhallabi (al-A'lam 3:34, d. 174 AH, 791 CE, Qayrawan; brother Yazid ibn Hatim linked) and Abd Allah ibn Yusuf al-Tinnisi (Ibn Hajar, Taqrib al-Tahdhib, p. 300 of the scan, d. 218 AH, 833 CE; the card had matched al-Jurjani d. 148 AH in al-A'lam). The cards for Zayn al-Abidin (card 14608, the Persian illustrator, not the fourth imam) and Ibrahim ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (dates 726-799 were al-Zuhri's) had been corrected in the meantime by packet corr-p1 and are kept as corrected. Left for outside research: Ahmad ibn Musa al-Kazim (no entry in al-A'lam or al-Wafi).
- **Yaqut sections for nine places (packet 54).** Sinjar, Farah, Daraa, Dastumaysan, Thaniyyat al-Wada, Qazvin, Kerman, Darabjird and al-Hadath gain a cited section in Arabic, English and Urdu summarising Yaqut's Mu'jam al-Buldan (Dar Sader), with the first English and Urdu pages for Qazvin and all three languages for Kerman; El-Tor was skipped because the entry does not clearly describe our town.
- Eight places gain a section on what Yaqut says of them in the Mu'jam al-Buldan, in Arabic, English and Urdu (Dumbawand, Ghumdan, Archidona, Manbasa, Awlil, Zabid, Yafa, Tartus), each cited by volume and page; Asbara and Alib are left out until their identity is settled.
- **One more person read from his dictionary entries (Lane B2, packet p03).** Abu Abd Allah ibn Mujahid al-Ta'i, the Ash'ari theologian who taught al-Baqillani kalam in Baghdad: Arabic, English and Urdu prose (draft, cited to al-Zirikli, al-A'lam vol. 5 p. 311, and al-Safadi, al-Wafi bi-l-Wafayat vol. 2 p. 35). Both entries are reported side by side and the year of death is given as each states it (370 AH, 980 CE, against about the 370s). Of the other nine in the packet, none could be read: seven have no entry in al-A'lam or al-Wafi, one is a different man in al-A'lam, and Tahmasp I already has prose; each is logged.
- **Yaqut sections for nine places (packet 51).** Khawash, al-Sarir, Qarnayn, Shakar, al-Baylaman, Tunkat, Mosul, Apamea and Palestine gain a short cited section in Arabic, English and Urdu summarising their entries in Yaqut al-Hamawi's Mu'jam al-Buldan (draft); Apamea and Palestine get their first prose pages. Hormuz was held back because Yaqut's Hurmuz may be the mainland port, not the island.
- **Sirat al-Hadi ila al-Haqq, pp. 206 to 215 (Lane A, batch 25): the meeting at Hadaqan, the fighting at Sana'a and the march through the south.** Fourteen event records, six persons and five places in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft, each cited to the printed page): al-Hadi's answer to Yazid al-Shakiri and Abu Rifa'a with the banner given at al-Ha'ira, the meeting and pledge of Abu al-Atahiya, the plundering of the baggage during the Friday sermon, the plea to the troops, al-Hadi's charge and his later regret for a word, the rout, the broken safety and the imprisonment of the leaders, Abu al-Atahiya's handing over and withdrawal, the governors sent and the levies lifted at Shibam and Bayt Dhukhar, the march to Samh and the woman's estate case, Dhamar, Hilan and al-Akhtut, Mankath, the Ja'afir and Jayshan, and Thath, Bashar and the return to Sana'a. A Zaydi source in the imam's followers' voice; praise, charges and rulings are attributed to the narrator with no verdict, abuse is not repeated, and the penalties are described as the book gives them. The page image (Apple Vision) recovered a line the OCR had dropped on p. 213.
- **Sirat al-Hadi ila al-Haqq, pp. 216 to 225 (Lane A, batch 26): the rising of Al Ya'fur and Al Tarif, Shibam, and al-Hadi's return to Sana'a.** Fourteen event records, four persons, one group and five places in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft, each cited to the printed page): the plot and the two men sent to Qudum with Sa'sa'a at al-Bawn, Ali ibn al-Abbas sent to Najr, the Qudumis' entry into Shibam and the killing of Ibn Abi Abbad, the rout and his burial, the rising at Zahr, Ibn Hanash and Ibn Harnud bringing al-Da'am and Abu al-Qasim, the rising of Ibn Mahfuz at Sana'a, the tribes' turning and the decision to leave Shibam, the freeing of As'ad ibn Abi Ya'fur and Ibrahim ibn Khalaf, the road to Raydah and Bayt Dhu'd, the fight at al-Ghayl in al-Bawn, Abdullah ibn al-Husayn's arrival and al-Da'am's excuse, the rout before Sana'a and the second entry. The four 288 AH events from the book's added first pages (Raydah, al-Rahba, the Sana'a rising, the Shibam rising) are cross-linked both ways, without being reconciled. A Zaydi source in the imam's followers' voice; charges, reasons and praise are attributed to the narrator with no verdict, and abuse is not repeated. Printed p. 223 is missing from the scanned file and is recorded as a gap.
- **Sirat al-Hadi ila al-Haqq, pp. 226 to 235 (Lane A, batch 27): the war of 288 AH at Sana'a and Banu al-Harith at Najran.** Eighteen event records, one person and four places in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft, each cited to the printed page): the people's wonder at al-Hadi's steadfastness and his prayer, safety for the people of Sana'a and the second Friday sermon, the fights at Ayman and Warraqatayn, Alab and Nuqm in Sha'ban and Ramadan, Banu al-Harith's coming down to Najran, the siege of al-Hajar and Muhammad ibn Ubaydallah's ten months at al-Hisn, the raid on the gate at the Fitr, the fight at Hidayn with the deaths of Ali ibn Sulayman and Abu al-Atahiya, the army of the day of sacrifice and the challenge to Ibn Khalaf, the night of safety and its breaking, and the sorties of 17 Dhu al-Hijja. A Zaydi source in the imam's followers' voice; wonder, prayers and charges against opponents are attributed to the narrator with no verdict, curses are not repeated, and book dates whose weekdays do not match the tabular calendar are given to the month. Printed p. 223 stays missing from the scan.
- **Sirat al-Hadi ila al-Haqq, pp. 236 to 245 (Lane A, batch 28): the end of the war of 289 AH at Sana'a, al-Hadi's leaving for Sa'da and the first marches of 290 AH.** Fourteen event records, three persons, three places and one group in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft, each cited to the printed page), and the sortie of 17 Dhu al-Hijja extended rather than duplicated: Abu al-Qasim's blow at Ibrahim ibn Khalaf, the Tabari reinforcement and the camp at Sabal, the raid on Zabwa and the death of Abu al-Qasim al-Ja'fari, al-Hadi's fall in the narrow pass and his son's defence, the fights at Dal', Zahr, Sabal, Adudan, Hadda and Ghayman, his leaving Sana'a for lack of funds, Najran and the pardon for Banu al-Harith, the hostages of Yam and Banu al-Harith, the marches on Allaf and on Wa'ila, and the appeal of Al Ya'fur and al-Da'am. A Zaydi source in the imam's followers' voice; praise, the word martyr and the imam's words to the people of Sana'a are attributed to the narrator with no verdict, and weekdays that do not match the tabular calendar are given to the month. The page images (Apple Vision) settled the place names; the text breaks off at the foot of p. 245.
- **Sirat al-Hadi ila al-Haqq, pp. 246 to 255 (Lane A, batch 29): the stay at Khiwan, the rout at Atwa and the imprisonment of Abu al-Qasim.** Twelve event records, four places and one person in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft, each cited to the printed page; the strife event of p. 245 now points on to the first new one): the meeting with the sons of Ya'fur at al-Ghayl, the wait at Bayt Dhu'd and Falj and the move to Sabal, the fights near Bayt Hadir and the withdrawal to Atwa, the attack of Al Tarif on the first of Rajab, al-Hadi hemmed in and the Tabaris' plea, Abu al-Qasim's capture and parade through Sana'a, Warwar and the news of Jaftam, the march on Amlah, Ibn Abbad and Banu Kulayb, Abu al-Qasim's chaining and move to Bayt Bus, the seizing of Jaftam at Arthal, and the verses the book ascribes to Abu al-Qasim. A Zaydi source in the imam's followers' voice; praise, the word martyrs, the charges against opponents and the verses are attributed to the narrator or poet with no verdict; the verses are described by sense and not reproduced, and the marginal heading on juristic benefits of the razing of Amlah is recorded without a ruling. Book weekdays that differ from the tabular calendar are given to the month. Why it matters: the museum now follows the imam's campaign of 290 AH to the point of his son's captivity.
- **Identity and date corrections on seven person cards (Lane B, packet corr-p1, 14 November 2026).** Each correction was read in a primary source before it was applied. Ibn al-Dahan the grammarian (Sa'id ibn al-Mubarak, Baghdad then Mosul) now carries his own dates, 494 to 569 AH, after the dates of his son, the poet Yahya (569 to 616 AH), had been written onto his card (Ibn Khallikan, al-Zirikli). Ibn Mattawayh loses a death date that the Encyclopaedia of Islam calls unreliable and is placed at Rayy as a pupil of Abd al-Jabbar. Zayn al-Abidin (work-14608) is recognised as the Safavid illustrator Zayn al-Abidin Tabrizi, not the fourth Imam, and loses the Imam's dates. Sa'id ibn al-Mubarak the hadith transmitter gets his death in 596 AH from al-Dhahabi and is kept apart from Ibn al-Dahan. Ibrahim ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas loses the dates of Ibrahim ibn Sa'd al-Zuhri, whom al-Bukhari lists separately. Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Tamirtashi keep their dates, now cited to al-A'lam with Hijri years, and the mismatching entries from an earlier batch are noted as not theirs.
- **Eight more people read from their dictionary entries (Lane B2, packet p02).** Short cited biographies in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft, each cited to volume and page): Ahmad ibn Uways al-Jalayiri, last Jalayirid sultan of Baghdad, and al-Murtada Muhammad ibn Yahya, a Zaydi imam of Sa'da (labelled as Zaydi), from al-Zirikli's al-A'lam (vol. 1 p. 101, vol. 7 p. 135); the Mughal emperor Jahangir (Encyclopaedia of Islam vol. 2 pp. 404-406), his wife Nur Jahan (vol. 8 pp. 135-136), the Seljuk sultan of Rum Kayqubad I (vol. 4 pp. 855-856) and Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur (vol. 1 p. 218, in the dynasty article); the Companion Rukana, from Ibn Hajar's al-Isaba (pp. 481-482) and Abu Nu'aym's Ma'rifat al-Sahaba (printed pp. 1113-1117), with the wrestling report, the divorce report and the verdicts on their chains attributed to their authors; and Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Qudama, father of Abu Umar and al-Muwaffaq, from Ibn Rajab's Dhayl (pp. 52, 61). The cards were corrected where the pages differed: Rukana's summary and places (Mecca and Medina, not Sind), a typo in al-Murtada's Arabic name, and Baghdad and Tabriz for Ahmad al-Jalayiri. Shah Jahan and Ageng Tirtayasa were skipped because no entry could be read.
- **Five of the most-linked people without prose now have cited biographies (Lane B2, packet p01), and al-Safadi's al-Wafi bi-l-Wafayat joins the sources.** New source record: al-Safadi, al-Wafi bi-l-Wafayat (Dar Ihya al-Turath, 2000). Arabic, English and Urdu prose (draft, each sentence cited to volume and page): Qadi Abd al-Jabbar (al-A'lam 3:273; al-Wafi 18:20-22; the Mu'tazili school is labelled before his position is stated and al-Safadi's hostile closing judgement is attributed to him alone), al-Najashi (al-A'lam 1:172, Imami labelled first), Mahmud Khattab al-Subki (al-A'lam 7:186), Musa ibn Shakir (al-A'lam 7:323) and Abu Bakr al-Marrudhi (al-A'lam 1:205; al-Wafi 7:256). Cards corrected to the entries: al-Subki born 1857 (1274 AH), not 1858; al-Najashi gains birth 982 and death 1058 and Baghdad; Abd al-Jabbar gains died_in Rayy, roles qadi and theologian; al-Marrudhi gains student_of Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Seven others in the packet were not found in a dictionary we hold and are logged as skipped.
- **Sirat al-Hadi ila al-Haqq, pp. 196 to 205 (Lane A, batch 24): the Kulaybis and Banu al-Harith after Allaf, and the march from Sa'da to Hadaqan.** Thirteen event records, five persons, three groups and three places in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft): Ibn Musbih's congratulation, Banu Kulayb's request for safety and their oath, the Akilis' removal to Banu Yajr, Ahmad ibn Abbad's refused request and journey to Iraq with the editor's two later reports, the imam's verse on the war, the raid of some of Banu al-Harith on Hamdan and al-Hadi's letter and verses to them, the march of Muharram 288 AH through al-Ha'ira, Khaywan, Athafit, Raydah and Madar to Hadaqan, and Abu al-Atahiya's letter and ambush order. A Zaydi source in the imam's followers' voice; praise, the marvel of the water and the charges against Al Tarif and the Jafatim are attributed to the narrator with no verdict, and verse is described, not quoted. Printed pages are footer-checked (offset 3); the account breaks off at the foot of p. 205.
- **First prose for ten more rulers, a family and a state card (packet 41).** The Sasanian house, Tahmasp I, al-Mansur Fakhr al-Din Uthman, Kayqubad I, Muhammad II the Aghlabid, Bahram Shah of Ghazna, Ahmad ibn Uways the Jalayirid, Sulayman II of Rum, Shah Jahan and Mansur II the Samanid gain Arabic, English and Urdu pages (draft). Fuller pages (Muhammad II, Bahram Shah, Sulayman II, Mansur II, Tahmasp) are cited to Hasan Ibrahim, Ibn al-Athir's Kamil and Salabi; the others are short pages stating only what the record and its named handbook give. Bahram Shah's death year is shown with the three differing dates (548 AH, 547 AH, 1157) and none preferred. Nomisma concepts record no linked coins for any of them; the concepts for al-Mansur Uthman and Kayqubad could not be fetched (server error) and are not described.
- **Sirat al-Hadi ila al-Haqq, pp. 185 to 195 (Lane A, batch 23): safety for Ibn Bustam, the razing of the Akili houses and the fight at Allaf.** Twelve event records, three persons, four groups and three places in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft, each cited to the printed page): Ibn al-Dahhak seeking safety through Abu al-Atahiya, the division of the spoils, Banu al-Harith asking safety, Ibn Bustam's safety and the leaving of Najran, the Akili houses and vines at Sa'da and Afqayn, the clash at Sam'in, the mid-Sha'ban night march, the charge at al-Sabra, al-Hadi's two poems, the raid at Afqayn and the fifth returned to the Mahadhir, the muster of 2 Ramadan 287 AH and the ascent of Allaf with the fall of al-Numays. A Zaydi account; marvels and rulings attributed to the narrator, verse described not quoted.
- **Gazetteer sections on eleven more place pages (packet 38).** Trapani, Tukra, Toledo, Tunis, Tus, Tustar, Ubeda, Valencia, Wahran, Xi'an and Zabid gain short cited Pleiades or iDAI.gazetteer sections in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft). Ubeda's iDAI section is left out because the record carries a different GeoNames id from ours; Sanaa, Babil and Askalan are founder-held and untouched.
- **Gazetteer sections on twelve more place pages (packet 37).** Shiraz, Sicily, Socotra, Tabarqa, Tabna, Tabriz, Tadmur (Palmyra), Taranto, Tayma, Tikrit, Tlemcen and Tournai gain a short cited Pleiades or iDAI.gazetteer section in Arabic, English and Urdu. Skipped: Sousse and Tortosa (their iDAI GeoNames id differs from ours).
- **Canon of Medicine, Fann 2 Ta'lim 3, urine chapters 2 to 4 (scan pp. 184 to 192): twenty-two concept records in Arabic, English and Urdu.** The colours of urine: the scales of yellow and red, colour in acute fevers and in jaundice, green urine (pistachio, verdigris, leek, sky blue), the kinds of black urine, how to tell their causes apart and the warnings drawn from them (with Rufus's saying and Ibn Sina's reply), white urine in its two senses, in fevers, in health and by temperament, the causes of red urine in cold diseases, red urine, urine like the washings of fresh meat, oily and purple urine; then consistency (thin, thick, thick clear against thin dyed, urine turning thick or clear, thick urine as a crisis and the bursting of swellings, forms of turbid urine, urine resembling an organ) and the smell of urine. Drafts with provenance, cited to printed pages of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya edition; garbled OCR lines on pp. 185 to 187, 189, 190 and 192 and the editor's footnotes were left out. The chapter on froth begins on p. 192.
- **Canon of Medicine, Fann 2 Ta'lim 3, urine chapters 5 to 13 (scan pp. 192 to 199): twenty-four concept records in Arabic, English and Urdu.** The foam of urine; sediment (the natural kind, in the sick and healthy, fat and lean, the unnatural kinds, sheet-like, bran-like and vetch-like, gruel-like, greasy, pus-like and raw, mucous, hairlike and leaven-like, gravelly and ashen, clotted, and what colour, position and time of settling show); abundant and scanty urine; matured healthy urine; urine by age, in men, women, pregnancy and after childbirth; animal urine and look-alike liquids; then the stool (amount, consistency, dryness, colour, black and green, form and timing). Drafts with provenance, cited to printed pages of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya edition; garbled OCR fragments on pp. 192, 193, 195 and 196, the English glosses and the editor's footnotes were left out. This ends Fann 2 Ta'lim 3; Fann 3 (the cause of health and disease and the necessity of death) begins on p. 200.
- **Canon of Medicine, Fann 3 (the cause of health and disease), the opening and Ta'lim 1 on upbringing, chapters 1 and 2 (scan pp. 200 to 211): twenty-one concept records in Arabic, English and Urdu.** Medicine as theoretical and practical and the two sciences of preserving health and treatment; the body's origin in seed and menstrual blood; the two afflictions of dissolution and putrefaction and the external and internal causes of drying; natural death and the lamp of innate heat; what preserving health can and cannot guarantee; the nutritive, pulsating and transformative powers; the seven matters to regulate; the care of the newborn (cord, salting, swaddling, bed, bathing); the mother's milk and first nursing; choosing a wet nurse, her food, the qualities and tests of good milk, correcting thick, thin, foul and scanty milk, her regimen and abstinence, how to nurse, weaning and first foods, and early movement and teething. Drafts with provenance, cited to printed pages of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya edition; one garbled line on p. 206 (a prohibition regarding nursing by an unfit woman) and the editor's footnotes on plants were left out. Chapter 3 (diseases of children) begins on p. 211.
- **Canon of Medicine, Fann 3, Ta'lim 2 (the common regimen of adults), chapters 1 to 6 (scan pp. 221 to 227): twenty-five concept records in Arabic, English and Urdu.** Exercise defined and why the body needs it, the harm of gathered residues, how exercise guards health, its kinds and qualities, the named exercises, grappling and the two-pegs exercise, varying exercise and exercising the chest and voice, gentle exercise for the weak and sick, riding in carts and boats, exercising the eye and ear, guarding a weak organ, when to begin and stop, rubbing and oiling before exercise, season and place, how long to exercise, keeping each day's diet and exercise steady; massage (kinds and aims, before and after exercise, recovery method and bedtime pressing); the bath for the healthy adult, the aims of bathing, cautions on leaving the bath, the bath's benefits and harms; and washing in cold water (who may, method and cautions). Drafts with provenance, cited to printed pages of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya edition; garbled OCR lines (p. 223 boat passage, p. 224 a clause on clearing the bowels, p. 225 an opening line, p. 226 two clauses on the bath, p. 227 one cold-bath sentence) and the editor's footnotes were left out. Chapter 7, on food, begins on p. 227.
- **Canon of Medicine, Fann 3, Ta'lim 2 (the common regimen of adults), chapter 7 on the management of food (scan pp. 227 to 236): twenty-five concept records in Arabic, English and Urdu.** Food for the healthy (meat, wheat, fruit; why pulses and fruit are not staples), eating only on true appetite, seasonal food and the harm of feast after famine, correcting a medicinal food eaten by mistake, surfeit and food on undigested food, stopping short of fullness, sleep posture and walking after a meal, the right measure of a meal and its signs, foods for each temperament, the order of foods in a meal, custom, country and body type, luxury eaters and mixed dishes, one meal or two, the empty stomach and the flow of bile, meals around exercise and the bath, drinking after food and enduring thirst, drink on food and sweets, overfilling and its remedies, food in old age, correcting hot, cold and thick foods, light and thick foods and the exerciser, fresh fruit and the watery humour, bad foods and their correctives, excess of each quality and the combinations the experienced warn against, and the ancients' meals with notes on dishes. Drafts with provenance, cited to printed pages of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya edition; garbled OCR fragments, the English glosses and the editor's footnotes were left out, and drink doses were not recorded. Chapter 8 (water and drink) begins on p. 236.
- **Canon of Medicine, Fann 3, Ta'lim 1, chapters 3 and 4 (diseases of children and the regimen of the growing child; scan pp. 211 to 220): twenty-five concept records in Arabic, English and Urdu.** Treating children through the wet nurse; gum and jaw swellings; loose bowels at teething; constipation; spasm and tetanus; cough and catarrh; poor breathing; thrush; ear discharge and earache; hot swelling of the brain; eye troubles from weeping; wrapping the nurse and sweating the infant; colic and repeated sneezing; pustules; navel protrusion, rupture and swelling at the cord; sleeplessness and what makes a child sleep; hiccough, vomiting and a weak stomach; frightening dreams; throat swelling and snoring; infantile convulsions and rectal prolapse; dysentery from cold; worms; abrasion of the thigh; then shaping the child's character and the growing child's day, schooling and regimen to fourteen. Drafts with provenance, cited to printed pages of the Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya edition; garbled OCR lines (the name of one illness on p. 216, the drug names for dysentery on p. 219, one gall-nut quantity on p. 215, a plant name on p. 217, one sentence on p. 212) and the editor's footnotes on plants were left out. This ends Ta'lim 1 on upbringing; Ta'lim 2, the common regimen of adults (exercise first), begins on p. 221.

## v1.30.0 — 2026-11-14
### Added
- **The Medicine Browser opens** (متصفح الطب النبوي والطب والتشريح والجراحة والدواء والتداوي في الإسلام) at `/{lang}/tibb/`, in Arabic, English and Urdu, with a card on the home page and an entry in the Explore menu. It gathers in one place everything the museum's sources say about six subjects: prophetic medicine, medicine and illness, anatomy, surgery, drugs, and seeking treatment. A reader can go from the verse on the healing in honey to the reports on cupping and black seed, to Ibn al-Qayyim's chapters in Zad al-Ma'ad, to a page of Ibn Sina's Canon, and to the record of the physician or the hospital, each with its source. The page opens with a view of its own, "the apothecary's jars": six shelves, one for each subject, with a jar for every remedy, disease or procedure the texts name — cupping, honey, black seed, fever, plague, the stages of creation, the treatment of wounds — filled to the level of how often the sources mention it. A jar with a gold lid opens the museum's record on it.
- **A medical text in any book harvested later appears by itself.** The browser finds its passages when the site is built, by a guarded word list, so nothing has to be tagged. The guards keep out the words that only look medical: the "disease" of the hypocrites' hearts, the protected pasture that is spelled like "fever", the "justice" that is spelled like the drug costus, the honey of Paradise, and the wounds of the compensation chapters.
- **The medicine dataset** at `/api/v1/tibb.json`, described in the OpenAPI file, `llms.txt` and the data guide: every record with its section, its subjects and the words that admitted it.
### Data
- **al-Thurayya links added to fifteen more places.** Jaffa, Yazd, Zanjan, Oran, Khujand, Tayma, Yanbu, Zarqa, Zubala, Zibatra and five more now point to their record in the al-Thurayya gazetteer, matched by exact Arabic name and by position within 7 km. This completes the al-Thurayya files whose names match one of our places, 343 in all, apart from the Ascalon place and ambiguous names.
- **Nomisma links added to Qalawun, Kayqubad I and Qaytbay.** Their Nomisma concept pages fail for names with an apostrophe, so each concept was read through Nomisma's query service instead and confirmed to name the same ruler.
- **Biblissima identifiers added to eighteen more scholars.** al-Busiri, Ibn Ajurrum, Qadi Iyad, Ibn Abi al-Hadid, al-Firuzabadi, Zakariyya al-Ansari, Ibn al-Salah, al-Sha'rani, Fakhr al-Din Iraqi, Sultan Walad, Juwayriyya bint al-Harith and seven more now carry their Biblissima record number, each accepted only because Biblissima's Wikidata link matches ours. Two further matches with year gaps join the founder's list in the progress note.
- **al-Thurayya links added to 25 further places.** Palmyra, Sidon, Sinjar, Siraf, Tabuk, Taif, Qus, Rashid (Rosetta), Shibam, Kandahar, Qinnasrin and fourteen more now point to their record in the al-Thurayya gazetteer, matched by exact Arabic name and by position within 7 km. Only the link and the source were added.
- **iDAI.gazetteer links added to 19 more places.** Sivas, Erzurum, Bitlis, Sinop, Izmir, Iskenderun, Aksum, Asilah, Qina, Mallawi, Kastamonu, Gebze and seven more now carry their German Archaeological Institute gazetteer number, each accepted only when exactly one populated place within 1.5 km matched our GeoNames number or Arabic name.
- **1,033 hadith reports on medicine** from the two Sahihs, the four Sunan and the Muwatta (the hadith-api Arabic editions), each a short excerpt with its collection and number: the Book of Medicine and the Book of the Sick, cupping, cautery, ruqya, honey, black seed, fever, plague, contagion, visiting the sick, the treatment of the wounded.
- **650 short excerpts from books already scanned and read by machine**: Zad al-Ma'ad, the two Dala'il al-Nubuwwa, Hilyat al-Awliya', al-Isaba, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Hayat al-Sahaba, Sifat al-Safwa, Ibn Sina's Canon, Ibn al-Nafis's Commentary on the Anatomy of the Canon and al-Razi's al-Hawi. Each is forty words at most, cited to its book and scan page; the machine-read text is not corrected, and every record is a draft until a human reads it.
- **230 existing records now belong to the browser**: physicians from al-Harith ibn Kalada and Rufayda al-Aslamiyya to al-Razi, Ibn Sina, al-Zahrawi and Ibn al-Nafis, the hospitals, the medical books, the plagues, the medical inventions and the fatwas on treatment.
- **New records with full prose in three languages**: prophetic medicine and its remedies (black seed, cautery, talbina, costus, senna, truffles, ithmid, fever, ladud and sa'ut), surgery, venesection, bone-setting, the care of the wounded in the Prophet's time, simple and compound drugs, and theriac and poisons, written from Zad al-Ma'ad, the Canon and the hadith collections with page and number.
### Tests
- The detector's rules are tested one by one (`scripts/tibb.test.ts`), and the founder's original request is kept with a production check-list in `docs/engineering/47-tibb-browser-requirements.md`.
## v1.29.1 — 2026-11-14
### Added
- **Du'a by occasion: comprehensive supplications.** The division of al-Adhkar on supplications for all times is open with one record: what al-Nawawi gathers on the merit of supplication and the short, all-embracing wordings from Sahih Muslim and the two Sahihs, each with its page.

### Changed
- **The museum's block on terrorist-organisation content now covers the full official designation lists.** The screening patterns behind the build's extremism check were compared, name by name, with the terrorist-organisation lists published by the European Union, the United States (State Department and Treasury), Canada, the United Nations Security Council, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, and every Islam-linked organisation on those lists that the check did not already catch is now caught — among them JNIM, the Abdallah Azzam Brigades, Al-Murabitoun, the Caucasus Emirate, Egyptian Islamic Jihad, the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan, Lashkar-e-Jhangvi and Hizbul Mujahideen, together with spelling variants that previously slipped through (GIA and the Gama'a al-Islamiyya, long named in the rule, are now actually matched). Nothing already in the museum was removed or changed: the collection is the golden reference, and the handful of designated names whose patterns would also catch records the founder has kept are documented in the content-safety rule for his decision.
### Data
- **Ten more persons read from al-Zirikli's al-A'lam.** Taha Surur, Muhammad Amin al-Shirwani (Sadreddinzade), Nuh ibn Mustafa, Ibn Abd al-Qawi al-Mardawi, Muhammad Abu Zahra, Sultan ibn Saif al-Ya'ribi (labelled Ibadi), Tawba al-Anbari, Abd al-Salam ibn Mashish, Ali ibn Ahmad al-Mahaimi and Ahmad ibn Kayghalagh now carry short cited biographies in Arabic, English and Urdu (draft), each from the entry itself with its volume and page. Four cards corrected to the entry: Ibn Abd al-Qawi died 1299 (not 1300), Sultan ibn Saif 1680 (not 1679), Ibn Mashish 1225 (not 1227), and Ibn Kayghalagh was born about 872 (not about 904); Abu Zahra is no longer described as a Maliki.

## v1.29.0 — 2026-11-13
### Added
- **Du'a by occasion: miscellaneous remembrances.** The division of al-Adhkar that gathers scattered chapters is open: the record on the manners of a gathering gains what al-Nawawi reports on the words said when rising from one, the supplication for those present, and the dislike of leaving without remembering God, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: guarding the tongue.** The division of al-Adhkar on speech is open: the record on guarding the tongue gains al-Nawawi's rule that one speaks only where the benefit is plain, and the reports he gathers for it from the two Sahihs and al-Tirmidhi, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: names.** The division of al-Adhkar on names is open: the record on naming gains al-Nawawi's chapters on the call to prayer in a newborn's ear, the prayer for blessing at the tahnik, the day of naming and the names he reports as dearest, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: marriage.** The division of al-Adhkar on marriage is open: the record on the marriage contract gains what al-Nawawi gathers on the address before the contract, the words said to the groom, and the supplication on the wedding night, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: greeting.** The division of al-Adhkar on greeting, asking leave and sneezing is open: the record on the greeting of peace gains al-Nawawi's reports on its merit, the best wording and reply, and his ruling on beginning and returning it, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: travel.** The division of al-Adhkar on the traveller is open with one record: what al-Nawawi gathers for setting out and for farewell, from consulting and istikhara to the words «أستودع الله دينك وأمانتك وخواتيم عملك» and the supplication for the traveller's piety, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: the campaign.** The division of al-Adhkar on the campaign is open with one record: what al-Nawawi gathers on asking sincerely for martyrdom, the supplication at the digging of the Trench and the pleading before battle, from the two Sahihs and the Sunan, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: breaking the fast.** The fasting division gains a third record: the record on iftar now carries the supplications al-Nawawi gathers for breaking the fast, with the books he assigns them to and their page.
- **Du'a by occasion: particular prayers.** The division of al-Adhkar on Friday and the two Eids is open: the records on the Friday prayer and on Eid al-Fitr gain what al-Nawawi says of the remembrances of Friday and its hour, and of the takbir of the two Eids, its times and its wordings, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: illness and death.** The division of al-Adhkar on illness is open: the record on visiting the sick gains what al-Nawawi gathers on what the sick person says and what is said to him, from the two Sahihs and the Sunan, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: matters that arise.** The division of al-Adhkar that opens with istikhara is open: the record on istikhara gains al-Nawawi's account of the supplication from Sahih al-Bukhari, the rulings he attaches to it, and his judgement on two weaker reports. One attribution in the section on asking blessing on the Prophet, added earlier today, is corrected to what the page gives (Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra).
- **Du'a by occasion: asking blessing on the Prophet.** The division of al-Adhkar on this is open: the existing record gains the reports al-Nawawi gathers on its merit and on doing so when he is mentioned, and his rejection of one added phrase, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: praising God.** The division of al-Adhkar on praise is open: the record on «الحمد لله» gains al-Nawawi's account of when praise is recommended, the report that a matter not begun with it is cut short, and the wording of the most complete praise, each with its page.
- **Du'a by occasion: reciting the Qur'an.** The division of al-Nawawi's al-Adhkar on recitation is open: the record on completing the Qur'an gains what he says of how often the early generations completed it, his own view that it depends on the person, and the times he prefers, each with its page.
- **The Du'a Browser can be read by occasion.** It was arranged only by where a supplication is found (the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the seerah, other books). It now also has "By occasion", following the divisions of al-Nawawi's al-Adhkar in the book's own order, with a page for each division that holds a record. The first sixteen records are written from the book itself, chapter by chapter: on waking, dressing, leaving and entering the house, the toilet, ablution, going to and entering the mosque, hearing the call to prayer, distress, fright, the new moon, the Night of Power, the talbiya, food, and the chief supplication for forgiveness. Each gives the reports al-Nawawi cites, the books he assigns them to and his own gradings, with the supplication in his wording and its page in the edition read (al-Arna'ut, Dar al-Fikr, 1994, on al-Maktaba al-Shamila). Six of the twenty divisions are open; the page says so. Arabic, English and Urdu; AI-written drafts, marked as such. In the API each du'a record carries its `occasion`.
- **Two verses the audit named now have their commentary.** 36:58 and 112:1 showed "no commentary filed yet", because the museum's digests of al-Tabari stop at the sixteenth volume of the Shakir edition. Their Tafsir sections now carry a digest written from the al-Turki edition (vol. 19, pp. 466-469; vol. 24, pp. 727-730), read on al-Maktaba al-Shamila: the grammarians' readings al-Tabari reports, the reports he cites and the reading he prefers, each sentence cited to its page. Two volume records and two source records for that edition are added, and the Tafsir Browser's volume list is headed "read by the museum" now that it spans two editions. Arabic, English and Urdu; AI text, labelled as such on the page.
- **The Tafsir Browser starts from the verse.** The page used to open with two lists, "Commentaries, 23 entries" and "Volumes, 16 entries", and the sixteen volumes were one work in one edition. It now opens with "Read by verse": the surahs that carry commentary, each with its count (al-Baqara: 284 of 286 verses), then the verses of the surah, then the commentary on the verse. From the landing to al-Tabari on 2:255 is two clicks. The surahs the digests have not reached are named as such. New pages: `/{lang}/tafsir/surah/<n>/` for the 14 surahs covered today.
- **Every verse page has a Tafsir section.** The 1,715 verses with a digest of al-Tabari had it inside "Place in the museum", unlabelled. The same paragraphs, unchanged, now stand under the heading Tafsir, with the commentator, the work and the volume cited, each a link. A verse with no digest says so in one sentence: how many commentaries the catalogue holds, which one is read verse by verse so far, and that it has not reached this verse. Nothing is borrowed from another verse.
- **Surah pages lead to their commentary.** The surah's record page and its surah map both carry "Tafsir on this surah" with the count of verses covered and a link to them.
- **`/{lang}/quran/` opens.** It answered "page not found". It is now a short door to the Mushaf, the Surah maps, the Tafsir Browser and the order of revelation. The Mushaf and the Surah maps each say in one sentence what the other is for.
- **The Signs of the Hour Browser is about the signs of the Hour.** It held all 2,621 eschatology records, most of what the Resurrection, Paradise and Fire browsers hold. Its landing now holds the 114 records about the signs and reads them in order: the signs in general, the Mahdi, the Dajjal, Yajuj and Majuj, the Hour itself, the museum's own records before the passages at each step. The page says the order is the customary one of the creed books and that no text fixes it. Nothing is deleted: the full index by source is at `/{lang}/signs/all/`, and all four landings carry the same short block saying what each browser holds.
- **Journeys have a front door.** The Explore menu opened one journey, the Hijra, and the other forty-nine could only be found in the class listing. `/{lang}/journeys/` lists all fifty by kind, each with its stations in order, and every journey page links back to the list and on to journeys of its kind.
- **Every Hijri month has an address.** `/{lang}/calendar/1447/9/` opens Ramadan 1447 as a plain page: its days with their Gregorian twins, its observances, and links to the month before and after; `/{lang}/calendar/1447/` lists the year's months. They exist for the ten years either side of the present Hijri year (1438 to 1458 AH today) and need no JavaScript. The calendar and the converter stay where they were, with links to the months under them.
- **A fatwa can be found from the question.** The Fatwa Explorer was the only browser of its family with no search box, and it was arranged by issuing institution alone. It now has a find box over all 345 fatwas and a "By subject" list: the 183 subjects the fatwas are about, taken from each fatwa's own record, each with its page. The list by source stays, one source to a page. Every one of these pages carries the same sentence: the museum records these fatwas as history and issues no ruling.
- **The Graph Explorer finds an entry by name.** Its box asked for an internal id such as `person/salah-al-din-yusuf-ibn-ayyub`. Typing "Saladin" now offers the entry and makes it the centre. The centres you have visited are listed above the chart with a way back; a filter that is still on is shown beside the box with one button to clear it; and when a name cannot be drawn the box says so itself, instead of a line under the chart.
- **The Time wing and the map take a typed year.** On the Time wing, a year in either calendar opens the century that holds it. On the map, a typed year moves the year bar, and the panel now says what the bar does: it lights the places with dated records in that year and names each region's era; it does not filter a place's own list.
- **Battles can be searched by name where you land.** The Battles landing has a find box over every battle record.
- **The Messengers and Prophets Browser draws the Prophets' Tree.** `/{lang}/messengers/` listed its twenty-five prophets as cards in a grid. It now opens with a drawn tree, Adam at the root and Muhammad at the crown, that can be read at a glance and explored: choosing a prophet lights his way down to the root and opens a card with the basis of his place, his recorded parents and ties, his summary, his mention counts and the link to his page. The tree states only what the graph holds. A solid branch is drawn only where a father-and-son edge is recorded (Ibrahim to Ismail and Ishaq, Ishaq to Ya'qub, Ya'qub to Yusuf, Dawud to Sulayman, Zakariyya to Yahya); the vine from Ismail to Muhammad is the Genealogies Browser's chain, dashed where the genealogists dispute it and solid where they agree; a prophet counted among the progeny in al-An'am 84 to 86 hangs on a dashed twig with the ayah linked; every other place is dotted and labelled as order of mention, not lineage. Every prophet on the tree is an ordinary link, so it works without JavaScript, and "Read the tree as text" gives the same content as a list. In Arabic, English and Urdu, light and dark, phone and desktop. The build fails if a drawn branch has no edge behind it.
- **Twelve browsers open with a view of their own.** Each of these pages used to open with the same grid of cards. Each now opens with a drawing made from its own records, in Arabic, English and Urdu, that can be read at a glance and explored by touch, mouse or keyboard, and that still works as plain links without JavaScript (`docs/site/signature-views.md`):
  - **Asma ul Husna**: the ninety-nine names as beads on one string of three turns, in al-Tirmidhi's order; a bead's core grows with the Qur'an passages linked to the name.
  - **Centuries, Years and Months**: the Hijri year as a wheel, a bar per month for the passages that mention it.
  - **Caliphs**: a lane per caliphate and a segment per reign on one axis in both calendars, so who reigned at the same time can be seen; rival claims are drawn as claims.
  - **Khutab and Durus**: the dated sermons on a Hijri timeline (undated ones in a tray, not placed), and a ring per lecturer for the series the museum holds.
  - **Battles**: the dated records per Hijri century, stacked by kind, and the Prophet's campaigns numbered in order of date on a map of Arabia.
  - **Journeys**: every route on one map, coloured and dashed by kind; choosing a journey brings its stations forward in order.
  - **Sacred Places**: a map of every located place, with magnified lenses on the surroundings of Mecca and Medina.
  - **Companions**: one dot per Companion by the Hijri decade of death; buttons light the Muhajirun, the Ansar, the Household, the Mothers of the Believers, the women or the Ten.
  - **Four Madhhabs**: the four schools as four columns on one time axis, each scholar a lifespan, each book a mark at its author's death, and teacher-to-student lines only where the graph records them.
  - **Fatwa**: the subjects people ask about as circles sized by the number of fatwas, each ringed by the sources that issued them.
  - **Tafsir**: the whole Mushaf as 114 blocks sized by verse count, filled where commentary exists, and re-orderable by order of revelation.
  - **Hadith Qudsi**: themes against the seven collections as a matrix of discs; choosing a disc lists its hadiths.
  Every view states only what the records hold: undated, unlocated and unlinked records are counted in the caption and never placed, and the build fails when a view's fixed layout no longer matches the data.
- **Every browser now opens with a view of its own.** Twenty-seven more browsers join the twelve above; each drawing is made from that browser's records, in Arabic, English and Urdu (`docs/site/signature-views.md`):
  - **Inventions**: a lane per field and a mark per invention at its first attestation, shaped by what became of it. **Jobs**: a market street of tiles sized by the people recorded in each occupation. **Screening Room**: a film strip of decades.
  - **Hisab**: the reward figures the cited texts give, on a ladder where each rung is ten times the one below; a reward stated without a number ends in an open arrow, never a figure. **Hasanat**: shelves of surahs and hadith collections where good deeds are named. **Sayyi'at**: the same question as a stream along the order of revelation.
  - **Paradise and the Fire**: one chart for both, surah by surah, each page lit on its own side. **Resurrection**: the three themes along the order of revelation. **Signs of the Hour**: a road of five stations in the customary order, said to be customary. **Ghayb**: eight doorways for its sections, with the Night Journey's stops as an ascent. **Angels**: a ring of offices drawn with plain discs.
  - **Nature**: six strata from the heavens to the sea. **Jinn & Devils**: which sections its records share. **Magic**: the terms the sources use and where two meet in one record.
  - **Akhlaq**: virtues and vices on two sides of one spine, dealings apart. **Ibadat**: a rosette of the acts of worship with the practice records as beads. **Du'a**: 114 lamps, lit for each surah in which a supplication is recorded.
  - **Miracles**: a loom joining each prophet to the themes of his signs. **Nubuwat**: seven themes as a seven-pointed chart. **Dreams**: constellations by source.
  - **Household of the Prophet**: a family chart drawn only from recorded kinship. **Family and Marriages**: the marriages on record as knots. **Genealogies**: the tribes as trees, only where the records link them.
  - **Mukatabat**: a flow from who sent a letter to where the museum found it. **Islamic Economy**: coin, deed and endowment on three dated ledgers. **Hudud**: a plain index of terms and references, with no ruling and no ranking.
  The same rule holds for all: what the records do not date, locate or link is counted in the caption and left off the drawing.

- **Lessons in the Education Explorer go deeper.** An Ontario educator who runs an Islamic school read the Explorer and said its content was "very surface level", and where the depth belonged: justice and morality as concepts in social studies, the scientists' understanding of the universe in science, and why each scientist did the work. A lesson page can now carry a depth layer after its cards and before "Try this": **Go deeper** (one scene or source excerpt seen closely), **Why they did it** (the scientist's stated purpose where a source preserves it, and a plain statement where none does), **Two views** and **Often misunderstood** (from Grade 6), **How do we know?** (from Grade 9), **Think about it** (one question that needs a reason, never recall) and **Into the museum** (doors into the people, places, objects and texts behind the lesson). Every factual sentence restates a museum record and carries that record's citation; every interpretive or religious statement names who holds it. A lesson without the layer looks exactly as before, and course structure, addresses, expectation codes and the draft label are unchanged. The standard is `docs/courses/depth-rubric.md`; `scripts/courses/check_depth.py` checks it.
- **The museum's measured reach is now logged in the repository.** `docs/status.md` gains a Reach section recording the Tranco ranking of islam.museum, read from Tranco's own API: #4,609,967 on the list of 23 October 2026, climbing daily to **#1,259,190 on the list of 13 November 2026** (checked 14 November) — up 69,207 places in a day and 259,190 places short of the top 1,000,000. The climb the outreach rests on is now written down in one place, with its source named, where the next checks can be appended. Documentation only; the site itself is unchanged.
